qt: to the Commission Idoia Villanueva Ruiz (The Left) Subject:

In November 2021, the Spanish Government announced the XCuenca project to close the regional railway line between Aranjuez, Cuenca and Utiel, which was opened between 1885 and 1947. The line was closed in July 2022, affecting 20 municipalities in three autonomous communities and four provinces. It provides a fundamental mobility service for local residents in an area with one of the most acute depopulation trends in Europe, limiting the area’s connections with the rest of Spain and Europe to only road transport. The closure has led to numerous demonstrations and protests – which are still taking place now – in the municipalities in question, including Aranjuez, Utiel and Cuenca. Concurrently, the European Parliament declared 2021 the European Year of Rail, with the aim of promoting train travel as a sustainable mobility alternative and contributing to the European Green Deal objective of achieving climate neutrality in 2025. In the light of this state of affairs: Does the Commission consider it acceptable that, while policies to boost rail transport are being pursued, the Spanish Government has decided, in a move at odds with the Commission’s mobility strategies, to close and dismantle lines of that kind?
at: (English version) to the Commission Idoia Villanueva Ruiz (The Left) (22 April 2024) Subject: Closure of the Aranjuez-Cuenca-Utiel regional railway line (Madrid-Cuenca-Valencia) In November 2021, the Spanish Government announced the XCuenca project to close the regional railway line between Aranjuez, Cuenca and Utiel, which was opened between 1885 and 1947. The line was closed in July 2022, affecting 20 municipalities in three autonomous communities and four provinces. It provides a fundamental mobility service for local residents in an area with one of the most acute depopulation trends in Europe, limiting the area’s connections with the rest of Spain and Europe to only road transport. The closure has led to numerous demonstrations and protests — which are still taking place now — in the municipalities in question, including Aranjuez, Utiel and Cuenca. Concurrently, the European Parliament declared 2021 the European Year of Rail, with the aim of promoting train travel as a sustainable mobility alternative and contributing to the European Green Deal objective of achieving climate neutrality in 2025. In the light of this state of affairs: Does the Commission consider it acceptable that, while policies to boost rail transport are being pursued, the Spanish Government has decided, in a move at odds with the Commission’s mobility strategies, to close and dismantle lines of that kind? (28 June 2024) The growth of rail transport, both for passengers and freight, is one of the primary objectives of the Sustainable and Smart Mobility Strategy (1), aimed at achieving sustainable and more efficient mobility. In this context, the Commission defends the presence of modern, reliable and efficient railway lines as part of the transEuropean transport network (TEN-T). Indeed, the only legal basis on which the EU could require a specific railway line to be maintained open is if it were part of the TEN-T network. However, this is not the case of the line in question. In the case of railway lines that are not part of the TEN-T, it is part of the Member States’ responsibilities for transport policy to assess the costs and benefits of their operation and decide on their potential closure. To favour the survival of small lines for which administrative requirements might be too high, EU law allows Member States to request exemptions from certain provisions of Directive 2012/34 (2). Those exemptions would allow to reduce administrative burden or simplify governance arrangements for local and regional railway infrastructures which do not have any strategic importance for the functioning of the railway market (3). If the reason for closing the line is a disproportionate administrative burden, Member States and local authorities responsible for transport policy may consider whether such exemption possibilities could allow the survival of these lines.

https://ec.europa.eu/info/law/better-regulation/have-your-say/initiatives/12438-Sustainable-and-Smart-Mobility-Strategy_en https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/dir/2012/34/oj Directive 2012/34, Article 2(4): Without prejudice to paragraph 3, Member States may exclude local and regional railway infrastructures which do not have any strategic importance for the functioning of the rail market from the application of Article 8(3) and local railway infrastructures which do not have any strategic importance for the functioning of the rail market from the application of Chapter IV. Member States shall notify the Commission of their intention to exclude such railway infrastructures. In accordance with the advisory procedure referred to in Article 62(2), the Commission shall decide whether such railway infrastructure may be considered to be without any strategic importance taking into account the length of railway lines concerned, their level of use and the traffic volume potentially impacted.
